title: The night song
hook: Sohila means song of praise; its five hymns close the day and close a life

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rehras close, and your line, both ends held. Did you keep a bookend at each end of the day? Today a new stretch begins: the last prayer before sleep. Day four hundred twenty-one.

Almost every family on earth has a bedtime song. A grandmother humming in the dark, a father singing the same three lines every night, badly, because the baby likes them. The words matter less than the fact that they're the last thing heard before sleep. The day has a lot of voices in it. The night song is the one that gets the final word. Sikhs have one too, and it's sung not only at the end of a day. Today: the night song.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER HUMMING IN THE DARK.` → `THE LAST THING HEARD BEFORE SLEEP.` → `THE NIGHT SONG GETS THE FINAL WORD.`

segments.voice: It's called Kirtan Sohila, or simply Sohila. Sohila is usually explained as a song of praise, and in old Punjabi it was also a word for joyful songs, the kind sung at weddings. It's short: five shabads, on pages twelve and thirteen of the Guru Granth Sahib, right after Rehras in the book. The first three are by Guru Nanak, the fourth by Guru Ram Das, the fifth by Guru Arjan. The Sikh code of conduct places it at night, before going to sleep. Many Sikhs say it in bed with the light off, or play it softly as children fall asleep. And it closes more than a day. When the Guru Granth Sahib is put to rest at night in many gurdwaras, Kirtan Sohila is recited. And when a Sikh dies, Kirtan Sohila is recited at the cremation, followed by Ardas. The same five hymns at bedtime and at a funeral. That's not gloomy. Many Sikhs describe sleep and death as both a kind of letting go, a handing of yourself back to the One, and the night song meets them with the same calm. The first hymn even speaks of a day fixed in advance, the way a wedding date is written, and the friends gathering to bless the one setting out. A song of joy for the night, and for the last night. Over the next two weeks we'll take the five hymns one at a time, each by its sound and then its meaning. Tonight, just know what it is. The night song.
screen: `SOHILA: A SONG OF PRAISE, OF JOY.` · `FIVE SHABADS, THREE GURUS, ANG 12–13.` · `BEFORE SLEEP, AND AT THE CREMATION.` · `SLEEP AND DEATH: HANDED BACK IN CALM.` · then, large: `THE NIGHT SONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read it before bed. Tonight, if you can find Kirtan Sohila on your phone, in a gutka, or as a recording, read or listen to it once, lying down, lights low. It takes only a few minutes. If you'd rather not tonight, picture yourself in bed, the day finished, and let one line you've learned on this path be the last thing you hear: anand bhaiaa, or hamree karo haath dai rachhaa. For now, rest. Let your body grow heavy, as if night has already come. The bell holds the time.
Sohila. Kirtan Sohila, the Sikh night song: five shabads of praise said before sleep, and recited at the end of a life.
Your line: the night song. Tonight, let the last thing you hear before sleep be chosen: Sohila, or one line from this path, instead of the phone. Day four hundred twenty-one.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sohilaa, a song of praise or joy; Kirtan Sohila is the Sikh night prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sohila is a sad prayer for the dead.
what it means: a song of praise and joy, said every night before sleep and also at the end of a life.
what a scholar hears: sohilaa was a word for joyful songs such as wedding songs; the first hymn's image of a wedding date written in advance shapes its use at both bedtime and cremation.
